lecture_context.lecture_title: Lecture 4: Adversarial Robustness and Generative Models

unit.name: Generative models as distribution matching
unit.description: Introduces generative modeling use cases, contrasts discriminative and generative learning, and states the probability-distribution matching goal.
unit.summary: The generative-modeling portion begins by listing uses such as text-to-image, video generation, privacy-preserving synthetic datasets, captioning, and code generation [ts=3015s]. The instructor contrasts discriminative models, which classify, with generative models, which aim to learn the underlying data distribution and create new samples [ts=3107s]. Generative models are framed as useful for simulation, creativity, and human-AI collaboration when they learn salient features from large datasets [ts=3131s]. The self-supervised intuition is that a model with fewer parameters than the amount of training data is forced to learn salient regularities rather than memorize every example [ts=3226s]. The probabilistic target is for the generated distribution to match the real data distribution, after which generated images follow the real-world distribution [ts=3272s].

key_points.text: Generative-model use cases include text-to-image synthesis, synthetic datasets, captioning, code generation, super-resolution, and inpainting.
Discriminative models classify examples, while generative models learn the underlying data distribution.
Generative models rely on large data so the model learns salient features rather than overfitting.
The core goal is to align the generated distribution with the real data distribution.
